claim: Translesion synthesis (TLS) is a highly conserved mutagenic DNA lesion tolerance pathway.
source: Translesion synthesis (TLS) is a highly conserved mutagenic DNA lesion tolerance pathway, which employs specialized, low-fidelity DNA polymerases to synthesize across lesions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TLS pathways.

claim: TLS employs specialized, low-fidelity DNA polymerases to synthesize across lesions.
source: Translesion synthesis (TLS) is a highly conserved mutagenic DNA lesion tolerance pathway, which employs specialized, low-fidelity DNA polymerases to synthesize across lesions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TLS mechanisms.

claim: Current models suggest that activity of specialized polymerases is predominantly associated with ongoing replication, functioning either at or behind the replication fork.
source: Current models suggest that activity of these polymerases is predominantly associated with ongoing replication, functioning either at or behind the replication fork.
evidence: This represents the prevailing understanding in the field based on existing literature.

claim: DnaE2 functions in DNA damage-dependent manner in replication-independent conditions.
source: Here we provide evidence for DNA damage-dependent function of a specialized polymerase, DnaE2, in replication-independent conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Components of the replication machinery localize on DNA in response to damage in non-replicating Caulobacter cells.
source: We develop an assay to follow lesion repair in non-replicating Caulobacter and observe that components of the replication machinery localize on DNA in response to damage.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing SSB, HolB, DnaN, and DnaE localizations after damage treatment.

claim: Replisome component localizations persist in the absence of DnaE2.
source: These localizations persist in the absence of DnaE2 or if catalytic activity of this polymerase is mutated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing persistent DnaN foci in ΔdnaE2 cells during damage recovery.

claim: Replisome component localizations persist if catalytic activity of DnaE2 is mutated.
source: These localizations persist in the absence of DnaE2 or if catalytic activity of this polymerase is mutated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing persistent DnaN foci in dnaE2* catalytic mutant cells.

claim: Single-stranded DNA gaps for SSB binding and low-fidelity polymerase-mediated synthesis are generated by nucleotide excision repair (NER).
source: Single-stranded DNA gaps for SSB binding and low-fidelity polymerase-mediated synthesis are generated by nucleotide excision repair (NER), as replisome components fail to localize in the absence of NER.
evidence: This is supported by data showing lack of DnaN and SSB foci in ΔuvrA cells.

claim: Replisome components fail to localize in the absence of NER.
source: Single-stranded DNA gaps for SSB binding and low-fidelity polymerase-mediated synthesis are generated by nucleotide excision repair (NER), as replisome components fail to localize in the absence of NER.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data showing absence of DnaN and SSB foci in ΔuvrA cells after damage.

claim: Gap-filling by DnaE2 facilitates cell cycle restoration when cells are released into replication-permissive conditions.
source: This mechanism of gap-filling facilitates cell cycle restoration when cells are released into replication-permissive conditions.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing division restoration in wild type but not ΔdnaE2 cells.

claim: Cross-talk between NER activity and specialized polymerases in gap-filling helps preserve genome integrity and enhances survival in a replication-independent manner.
source: Thus, such cross-talk (between activity of NER and specialized polymerases in subsequent gap-filling) helps preserve genome integrity and enhances survival in a replication-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by survival assays showing enhanced fraction survival in wild type cells with recovery time compared to ΔdnaE2 cells.

claim: Bulky lesions such as those caused by UV light (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, CPD and 6,4 photoproducts, 6-4PP) are predominantly repaired by nucleotide excision repair (NER) in all domains of life.
source: In all domains of life, bulky lesions such as those caused by UV light (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, CPD and to a lesser extent 6,4 photoproducts, 6-4PP) are predominantly repaired by nucleotide excision repair (NER) (Boyce and Howard-Flanders, 1964; Chatterjee and Walker, 2017; Kisker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on NER mechanisms.

claim: NER can function in global genomic repair (GGR) via surveilling the DNA double-helix for distortions.
source: This pathway can function in global genomic repair (GGR) via surveilling the DNA double-helix for distortions or more specifically via transcription-coupled repair (TCR) (Kisker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on NER pathways.

claim: NER can function via transcription-coupled repair (TCR).
source: This pathway can function in global genomic repair (GGR) via surveilling the DNA double-helix for distortions or more specifically via transcription-coupled repair (TCR) (Kisker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on NER pathways.

claim: The main steps of NER involve lesion detection followed by incision of few bases upstream and downstream of the lesion, resulting in removal of a short stretch of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).
source: The main steps of NER involve lesion detection followed by incision of few bases upstream and downstream of the lesion, resulting in removal of a short stretch of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NER mechanism.

claim: In some cases, NER can result in generation of longer patches of ssDNA.
source: In some cases, NER can also result in generation of longer patches of ssDNA (Cooper, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ssDNA gaps generated by NER are filled by synthesis from a DNA polymerase.
source: ssDNA gaps are then filled by synthesis from a DNA polymerase (Kisker et al., 2013; Sancar and Rupp, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on NER.

claim: The NER-mediated damage removal pathway is largely error-free.
source: While the NER-mediated damage removal pathway is largely error-free, lesions encountered by the replication machinery (e.g., CPDs, 6-4PPs, and cross-links such as those generated by antibiotics including mitomycin C [MMC]) can also be dealt with via error-prone translesion synthesis (TLS) (Chatterjee and Walker, 2017; Fuchs and Fujii, 2013; Fujii and Fuchs, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Lesions encountered by the replication machinery can be dealt with via error-prone translesion synthesis (TLS).
source: While the NER-mediated damage removal pathway is largely error-free, lesions encountered by the replication machinery (e.g., CPDs, 6-4PPs, and cross-links such as those generated by antibiotics including mitomycin C [MMC]) can also be dealt with via error-prone translesion synthesis (TLS) (Chatterjee and Walker, 2017; Fuchs and Fujii, 2013; Fujii and Fuchs, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on TLS.

claim: TLS employs low-fidelity polymerases to synthesize across DNA lesions, with increased likelihood of mutagenesis during this process.
source: TLS employs low-fidelity polymerases to synthesize across DNA lesions, with increased likelihood of mutagenesis during this process (Fuchs and Fujii, 2013; Galhardo et al., 2005; Kato and Shinoura, 1977; Nohmi et al., 1988; Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on TLS mechanisms.

claim: In most bacteria, expression of specialized polymerases is regulated by the SOS response.
source: In most bacteria, expression of these polymerases is regulated by the SOS response, which is activated by the RecA-nucleoprotein filament under DNA damage (Baharoglu and Mazel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on SOS response.

claim: The SOS response is activated by the RecA-nucleoprotein filament under DNA damage.
source: In most bacteria, expression of these polymerases is regulated by the SOS response, which is activated by the RecA-nucleoprotein filament under DNA damage (Baharoglu and Mazel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on SOS response.

claim: E. coli specialized Y-family polymerases DinB (PolIV) and UmuDC (PolV) function in DNA lesion tolerance and contribute to mutagenesis in several bacterial systems.
source: Currently, most of our understanding about TLS comes from studies on specialized Y-family polymerases of E. coli, DinB (PolIV) and UmuDC (PolV), both of which function in DNA lesion tolerance and contribute to mutagenesis in several bacterial systems (Kato and Shinoura, 1977; Nohmi et al., 1988; Steinborn, 1978; Sung et al., 2003; Wagner et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on E. coli TLS polymerases.

claim: PolV has been implicated in RecA-dependent post-replicative gap-filling activity.
source: In addition, PolV has also been implicated in RecA-dependent post-replicative gap-filling activity (Isogawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus, Mycobacterium sp., and Pseudomonas sp. encode an alternate, SOS-inducible error-prone polymerase, DnaE2.
source: In contrast to E. coli, Caulobacter crescentus as well as other bacteria including Mycobacterium sp. and Pseudomonas sp. encode an alternate, SOS-inducible error-prone polymerase, DnaE2 (Boshoff et al., 2003; Galhardo et al., 2005; Jatsenko et al., 2017; Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on DnaE2 in various bacterial species.

claim: DnaE2 is highly conserved and is mutually exclusive with PolV in occurrence.
source: DnaE2 is highly conserved and is mutually exclusive with PolV in occurrence.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis cited in the literature.

claim: In organisms where DnaE2 has been studied, it is the primary TLS polymerase and the only contributor to damage-induced mutagenesis.
source: In the limited organisms where DnaE2 has been studied so far, it is the primary TLS polymerase and the only contributor to damage-induced mutagenesis (Alves et al., 2017; Galhardo et al., 2005; Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on DnaE2 function.

claim: DnaE2 is thought to preferentially act on MMC-induced damage, where it contributes to all induced mutagenesis observed.
source: In contrast to PolV, DnaE2 is thought to preferentially act on MMC-induced damage, where it contributes to all induced mutagenesis observed (Galhardo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study on DnaE2 function in Caulobacter.

claim: In case of UV damage, there are uncharacterized mechanisms that can contribute to damage tolerance and mutagenesis that are independent of DnaE2.
source: In case of UV, there are still uncharacterized mechanisms that can contribute to damage tolerance and mutagenesis that are independent of DnaE2 (Galhardo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: DnaE2 co-occurs with ImuB, a protein that carries a β-clamp binding motif.
source: DnaE2 co-occurs with ImuB, a protein that carries a β-clamp binding motif, and is thought to act as a bridge between DnaE2 and the replisome (Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on DnaE2-ImuB interaction.

claim: ImuB is thought to act as a bridge between DnaE2 and the replisome.
source: DnaE2 co-occurs with ImuB, a protein that carries a β-clamp binding motif, and is thought to act as a bridge between DnaE2 and the replisome (Warner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents a proposed model.

claim: In vivo investigations of DnaE2 function in damage tolerance and cellular survival are limited.
source: Unlike E. coli, where activities of PolIV and PolV are well-studied, in vivo investigations of DnaE2 function in damage tolerance and cellular survival are limited.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the literature.

claim: Error-prone polymerases can synthesize DNA and their activity is mediated by interaction with the β-clamp of the replisome.
source: Since error-prone polymerases can synthesize DNA and their activity is mediated by interaction with the β-clamp of the replisome (Bunting et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2019; Fujii and Fuchs, 2004; Thrall et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2009; Warner et al., 2010), action of these polymerases has mostly been studied in the context of replicating cells, as a mechanism that facilitates continued DNA synthesis by acting at or behind the replication fork (Chang et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Indiani et al., 2005; Jeiranian et al., 2013; Marians, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on polymerase-clamp interactions.

claim: Action of error-prone polymerases has mostly been studied in the context of replicating cells, as a mechanism that facilitates continued DNA synthesis by acting at or behind the replication fork.
source: Since error-prone polymerases can synthesize DNA and their activity is mediated by interaction with the β-clamp of the replisome (Bunting et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2019; Fujii and Fuchs, 2004; Thrall et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2009; Warner et al., 2010), action of these polymerases has mostly been studied in the context of replicating cells, as a mechanism that facilitates continued DNA synthesis by acting at or behind the replication fork (Chang et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Indiani et al., 2005; Jeiranian et al., 2013; Marians, 2018).
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the literature supported by citations.

claim: Some studies have proposed the possibility of error-prone synthesis in a manner that is replication-independent.
source: In addition to replication-associated lesion tolerance, some studies have proposed the possibility of error-prone synthesis in a manner that is replication-independent (Janel-Bintz et al., 2017; Kozmin and Jinks-Robertson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells can undergo stationary phase mutagenesis that is dependent on action of error-prone polymerases.
source: This is supported by observations that cells can undergo stationary phase mutagenesis that is dependent on action of error-prone polymerases (Bull et al., 2001; Corzett et al., 2013; Janel-Bintz et al., 2017; Sung et al., 2003; Yeiser et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on stationary phase mutagenesis.

claim: Microscopy-based approaches have provided evidence that tolerance or gap-filling could occur outside the context of the replication fork in E. coli.
source: Microscopy-based approaches have also provided evidence in line with the idea that tolerance or gap-filling could occur outside the context of the replication fork in E. coli, as replisome components, such as the β-clamp, as well as specialized polymerases (PolIV and PolV) were found to localize away from the fork in response to DNA damage (Henrikus et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2015; Soubry et al., 2019; Thrall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous microscopy studies in E. coli.

claim: Replisome components and specialized polymerases were found to localize away from the fork in response to DNA damage in E. coli.
source: Microscopy-based approaches have also provided evidence in line with the idea that tolerance or gap-filling could occur outside the context of the replication fork in E. coli, as replisome components, such as the β-clamp, as well as specialized polymerases (PolIV and PolV) were found to localize away from the fork in response to DNA damage (Henrikus et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2015; Soubry et al., 2019; Thrall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous microscopy studies.

claim: Recent studies suggest cross-talk between specialized polymerases and NER in E. coli, yeast, and human cells.
source: Furthermore, while originally considered as distinct mechanisms of repair (damage tolerance vs. damage removal), recent studies also suggest cross-talk between specialized polymerases and NER in E. coli, yeast, and human cells (Giannattasio et al., 2010; Janel-Bintz et al., 2017; Kozmin and Jinks-Robertson, 2013; Sertic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies in multiple organisms.

claim: Long-standing observations suggest that NER can be mutagenic under certain conditions in E. coli, in a manner that is dependent on RecA.
source: Indeed, long-standing observations suggest that NER can be mutagenic under certain conditions in E. coli, in a manner that is dependent on RecA (Bridges and Mottershead, 1971; Cohen-Fix and Livneh, 1994; Nishioka and Doudney, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to older literature on mutagenic NER.

claim: The mechanistic basis of replication-independent lesion repair and its conservation across bacteria that encode diverse specialized polymerases remains to be elucidated.
source: However, the mechanistic basis of this process in replication-independent conditions and conservation of the same across bacteria that encode diverse specialized polymerases remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is an assessment of gaps in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Several bacterial systems undergo nonoverlapping cycles of DNA replication and have distinct cell cycle phases with no ongoing DNA synthesis.
source: For example, unlike E. coli, several bacterial systems undergo nonoverlapping cycles of DNA replication and have distinct cell cycle phases with no ongoing DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell cycle diversity.

claim: The relevance of lesion correction or gap-filling for genome integrity maintenance in the absence of an active replication fork is relatively less explored, especially in bacterial contexts.
source: The relevance of lesion correction or gap-filling for genome integrity maintenance in the absence of an active replication fork (such as in non-replicating swarming cells) is relatively less explored, especially in bacterial contexts.
evidence: This is an assessment of gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Caulobacter is well-suited to study activity of specialized polymerases due to its distinct cell cycle.
source: Caulobacter is well-suited to study activity of these specialized polymerases due to its distinct cell cycle.
evidence: This is a rationale for the experimental system choice.

claim: Every Caulobacter cell division gives rise to two different cell types: a stalked and a swarmer cell.
source: Every cell division gives rise to two different cell types: a stalked and a swarmer cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Caulobacter cell cycle.

claim: The stalked Caulobacter cell initiates replication soon after division.
source: While the stalked cell initiates replication soon after division, a swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before replication reinitiation (Schrader and Shapiro, 2015) and hence swarmers can represent a pool of naturally occurring non-replicating cells in the environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Caulobacter cell cycle supported by citation.

claim: A Caulobacter swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before replication reinitiation.
source: While the stalked cell initiates replication soon after division, a swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before replication reinitiation (Schrader and Shapiro, 2015) and hence swarmers can represent a pool of naturally occurring non-replicating cells in the environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Caulobacter cell cycle supported by citation.

claim: Caulobacter swarmers can represent a pool of naturally occurring non-replicating cells in the environment.
source: While the stalked cell initiates replication soon after division, a swarmer cell must differentiate into a stalked cell before replication reinitiation (Schrader and Shapiro, 2015) and hence swarmers can represent a pool of naturally occurring non-replicating cells in the environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of Caulobacter cell cycle.

claim: Under laboratory conditions, Caulobacter swarmer cells can be isolated via density-gradient centrifugation and replication initiation can be inhibited, resulting in a population of non-replicating cells with a single chromosome.
source: Under laboratory conditions, these swarmer cells can be isolated via density-gradient centrifugation and replication initiation can be inhibited, resulting in a population of non-replicating cells with a single chromosome (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015; Schrader and Shapiro, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Low-fidelity polymerase DnaE2 functions in gap-filling damaged DNA in non-replicating Caulobacter cells.
source: We show that low-fidelity polymerase DnaE2 functions in gap-filling damaged DNA in non-replicating cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data showing persistent foci in ΔdnaE2 cells.

claim: Gap-filling by DnaE2 is facilitated by de novo loading of replisome components at long ssDNA gaps likely generated by a subset of NER events.
source: This is facilitated by de novo loading of replisome components (SSB, HolB [part of the clamp loader complex], β-clamp, and replicative polymerase) at long ssDNA gaps likely generated by a subset of NER events.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing replisome component localizations that are dependent on NER.

claim: DnaE2-mediated gap-filling in non-replicating cells promotes cell cycle restoration and cell division when cells are released into replication-permissive conditions.
source: We find that this form of gap-filling in non-replicating cells promotes cell cycle restoration and cell division, upon release into replication-permissive conditions.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging and survival assay data.

claim: The study provides in vivo evidence for a novel function of DnaE2 that is spatially and temporally separated from the active replication fork.
source: Our study provides in vivo evidence for a novel function of DnaE2 that is spatially and temporally separated from the active replication fork.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental system and data.

claim: Coordinated activity of NER and low-fidelity polymerases can serve as a potential mechanism through which non-replicating cells increase their chances of survival under damage.
source: Given that DNA damage can occur in any cell type whether actively replicating or not, coordinated activity of NER and low-fidelity polymerases can serve as a potential mechanism through which non-replicating cells such as bacteria in stationary phase or cells in other differentiated phases increase their chances of survival under damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing enhanced survival with DnaE2-mediated gap-filling.

claim: Flow cytometry profiles confirmed the presence of a single chromosome in non-replicating swarmer cells during the course of the entire experiment.
source: Flow cytometry profiles of cells confirmed the presence of a single chromosome during the course of the entire experiment (Figure 1A, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fluorescent fusions to Caulobacter β-clamp (DnaN), HolB, PolIII (DnaE), and SSB did not perturb the function of the proteins as cells displayed wild type growth dynamics in steady-state conditions.
source: These fusions did not perturb the function of the proteins as cells displayed wild type growth dynamics in steady-state conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B 'control').
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Fluorescent fusions to replisome components did not show increased sensitivity to DNA damage treatment via MMC or UV.
source: They also did not show increased sensitivity to DNA damage treatment via MMC or UV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data under damage conditions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Fluorescently-tagged replisome components localized on DNA in actively replicating Caulobacter cells.
source: The fusion proteins localized on DNA in actively replicating cells (Figure 1B, +replication), and as anticipated, their localizations gradually shifted from one pole to the other within one cycle of DNA replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Localizations of fluorescently-tagged replisome components gradually shifted from one pole to the other within one cycle of DNA replication in Caulobacter.
source: The fusion proteins localized on DNA in actively replicating cells (Figure 1B, +replication), and as anticipated, their localizations gradually shifted from one pole to the other within one cycle of DNA replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Observations of replisome dynamics are in line with previous reports in Caulobacter crescentus, Bacillus subtilis, and E. coli.
source: These observations are in line with previous reports of replisome dynamics in several bacterial systems including Caulobacter crescentus, Bacillus subtilis, and E. coli (Aakre et al., 2013; Collier and Shapiro, 2009; Jensen et al., 2001; Lemon and Grossman, 1998; Mangiameli et al., 2017; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on replisome dynamics.

claim: Replication-inhibited Caulobacter swarmer cells were devoid of replisome foci.
source: In contrast to actively replicating cells, replication-inhibited swarmer cells were devoid of replisome foci (Figure 1B), consistent with the idea that the localization of replisome components is indicative of active DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The localization of replisome components is indicative of active DNA replication in Caulobacter.
source: In contrast to actively replicating cells, replication-inhibited swarmer cells were devoid of replisome foci (Figure 1B), consistent with the idea that the localization of replisome components is indicative of active DNA replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that replisome foci are absent in non-replicating cells.

claim: MMC is a naturally produced antibiotic that acts predominantly on the guanine residue of DNA, making three major forms of damage: mono-adducts, intra-strand cross-links, and inter-strand cross-links.
source: MMC is a naturally produced antibiotic that acts predominantly on the guanine residue of DNA, making three major forms of damage: mono-adducts, intra-strand cross-links, and inter-strand cross-links (Bargonetti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MMC mechanism supported by citation.

claim: In Caulobacter, DnaE2 preferentially acts on MMC-induced damage as all mutagenesis associated with MMC treatment is mediated via action of this specialized polymerase.
source: In case of Caulobacter, it is thought that DnaE2 preferentially acts on MMC-induced damage as all mutagenesis associated with MMC treatment is mediated via action of this specialized polymerase; in absence of the polymerase, cells show high sensitivity to MMC treatment (Galhardo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study on DnaE2 function in Caulobacter.

claim: In absence of DnaE2, Caulobacter cells show high sensitivity to MMC treatment.
source: In case of Caulobacter, it is thought that DnaE2 preferentially acts on MMC-induced damage as all mutagenesis associated with MMC treatment is mediated via action of this specialized polymerase; in absence of the polymerase, cells show high sensitivity to MMC treatment (Galhardo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study and confirmed by data in this study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: DNA damage treatment resulted in the formation of β-clamp foci in non-replicating Caulobacter swarmer cells.
source: We found that DNA damage treatment resulted in the formation of β-clamp foci in non-replicating cells (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: DNA damage treatment resulted in the formation of foci for other replisome components (SSB, HolB, DnaE) in non-replicating cells.
source: This was found to be the case for other replisome components as well (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The percentage of cells with damage-induced β-clamp foci increased with increasing doses of MMC.
source: The percentage of cells with damage-induced β-clamp foci increased with increasing doses of MMC. At 0.125 µg/ml MMC treatment, 9% cells had β-clamp foci, while at higher doses of 0.75 µg/ml MMC, foci were observed in 59% cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Percentage of cells with DnaN localizations gradually decreased with time during damage recovery in non-replicating cells.
source: Consistent with the possibility of dissociation during recovery, we found that percentage of cells with DnaN localizations gradually decreased with time (Figure 2C) and across all doses of damage tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: After 30 min of 0.5 µg/ml MMC treatment, 52% cells on average had DnaN localization and at 90 min after damage removal, the number reduced to 30%.
source: For example, after 30 min of 0.5 µg/ml MMC treatment, 52% cells on average had DnaN localization and at 90 min after damage removal, the number reduced to 30%.
evidence: This is quantification from microscopy data.

claim: The pattern of localization after damage treatment, followed by reduction in percentage of cells with foci during recovery was also observed for SSB, HolB, and DnaE.
source: This pattern of localization after damage treatment, followed by reduction in percentage of cells with foci during recovery was also observed in the case of SSB, HolB, and DnaE (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells had more SSB localizations on average than DnaN.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that cells had more SSB localizations on average than DnaN. 14% cells had ≥2 DnaN foci after MMC treatment, while 37% cells harbored ≥2 SSB localizations.
evidence: This is quantification from microscopy data.

claim: 14% cells had ≥2 DnaN foci after MMC treatment, while 37% cells harbored ≥2 SSB localizations.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that cells had more SSB localizations on average than DnaN. 14% cells had ≥2 DnaN foci after MMC treatment, while 37% cells harbored ≥2 SSB localizations.
evidence: This is quantification from microscopy data.

claim: 90% of DnaN foci colocalized with SSB (with distance of a DnaN focus from the nearest SSB localization being within 300 nm).
source: Assessment of the extent of colocalization between DnaN and SSB further showed that 90% of DnaN foci colocalized with SSB (with distance of a DnaN focus from the nearest SSB localization being within 300 nm), while only 51% of SSB foci colocalized with DnaN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that not all SSB may be associated with the β-clamp or that SSB could precede β-clamp localization.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Only 51% of SSB foci colocalized with DnaN.
source: Assessment of the extent of colocalization between DnaN and SSB further showed that 90% of DnaN foci colocalized with SSB (with distance of a DnaN focus from the nearest SSB localization being within 300 nm), while only 51% of SSB foci colocalized with DnaN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that not all SSB may be associated with the β-clamp or that SSB could precede β-clamp localization.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Not all SSB may be associated with the β-clamp or SSB could precede β-clamp localization.
source: Assessment of the extent of colocalization between DnaN and SSB further showed that 90% of DnaN foci colocalized with SSB (with distance of a DnaN focus from the nearest SSB localization being within 300 nm), while only 51% of SSB foci colocalized with DnaN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that not all SSB may be associated with the β-clamp or that SSB could precede β-clamp localization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data.

claim: Exposure of cells to two doses of UV damage (75 and 150 J/m2) resulted in localization and subsequent reduction in percentage of cells with replisome foci during recovery.
source: Exposure of cells to two doses of UV damage (75 and 150 J/m2) also resulted localization and subsequent reduction in percentage of cells with replisome foci during recovery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F, G.

claim: SSB, along with components of the PolIIIHE, including the clamp-loader, β-clamp, and the replicative polymerase, associates with DNA during damage even in the absence of ongoing replication.
source: Taken together, these data support the idea that SSB, along with components of the PolIIIHE, including the clamp-loader, β-clamp, and the replicative polymerase, associates with DNA during damage even in the absence of ongoing replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy data showing replisome component localizations in non-replicating cells.

claim: Decrease in localizations over time could be indicative of potential repair in non-replicating cells.
source: Decrease in localizations over time could be indicative of potential repair in non-replicating cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of decreasing foci over time.

claim: SSB foci under non-replicating conditions indicate the presence of ssDNA stretches long enough to accommodate SSB tetramers (30 nt or more).
source: SSB foci under these conditions indicate the presence of ssDNA stretches long enough to accommodate SSB tetramers (30 nt or more) (Bell et al., 2015; Lohman and Ferrari, 1994).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about SSB binding properties supported by citations.

claim: In replicating cells, ssDNA tracts are thought to be generated as a result of helicase activity that continues to unwind double-stranded DNA ahead of the replisome that has encountered a lesion.
source: In replicating cells, ssDNA tracts are thought to be generated as a result of helicase activity that continues to unwind double-stranded DNA ahead of the replisome that has encountered a lesion (Belle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ssDNA generation during replication supported by citation.

claim: Non-replicating Caulobacter cells activated the DNA damage response after MMC exposure.
source: We found that non-replicating cells activated the DNA damage response after MMC exposure, providing further evidence for the formation of ssDNA gaps in such conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by SOS reporter data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deletion of the SOS activator, recA, did not perturb localization of DnaN under damage in non-replicating cells.
source: Deletion of the SOS activator, recA, did not perturb localization of DnaN under damage. However, RecA was essential for dissociation during damage recovery as DnaN foci persisted in non-replicating cells lacking recA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RecA was essential for dissociation of DnaN during damage recovery as DnaN foci persisted in non-replicating cells lacking recA.
source: Deletion of the SOS activator, recA, did not perturb localization of DnaN under damage. However, RecA was essential for dissociation during damage recovery as DnaN foci persisted in non-replicating cells lacking recA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A RecA-independent pathway is required for regulating the association of replisome components with DNA in cells that are not undergoing active DNA synthesis.
source: These observations suggest that a RecA-independent pathway is required for regulating the association of replisome components with DNA in cells that are not undergoing active DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that DnaN localizes in ΔrecA cells.

claim: Non-replicating cells with deletion of uvrA did not form DnaN foci under MMC or UV damage.
source: We observed that non-replicating cells with deletion of uvrA (part of the NER pathway) did not form DnaN foci under MMC or UV damage (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lesion processing by NER alone results in the formation of ssDNA gaps on which replisome components can localize in non-replicating cells.
source: Thus, our data suggest that lesion processing by NER alone results in the formation of ssDNA gaps on which replisome components can localize in non-replicating cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that ΔuvrA cells lack replisome foci.

claim: Cells without NER (ΔuvrA) were deficient in SOS induction.
source: Furthermore, cells without NER were deficient in SOS induction (Figure 3D), suggesting that NER-mediated gap generation serves two functions: (a) providing ssDNA substrate for recruitment of SSB and other replisome components to these regions and (b) induction of the SOS response.
evidence: This is supported by SOS reporter data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NER-mediated gap generation serves two functions: (a) providing ssDNA substrate for recruitment of SSB and other replisome components to these regions and (b) induction of the SOS response.
source: Furthermore, cells without NER were deficient in SOS induction (Figure 3D), suggesting that NER-mediated gap generation serves two functions: (a) providing ssDNA substrate for recruitment of SSB and other replisome components to these regions and (b) induction of the SOS response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observations that ΔuvrA cells lack both replisome foci and SOS induction.

claim: NER-mediated gap generation facilitates ssDNA gap-filling in non-replicating Caulobacter.
source: Together, this facilitates ssDNA gap-filling in non-replicating Caulobacter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing NER-dependent replisome localization and SOS induction.

claim: The experimental setup of non-replicating swarmer cells (with a single chromosome) does not permit gap-filling by recombination, due to absence of a homologous template for repair.
source: We ruled out a role for homologous recombination in this process as our experimental setup of non-replicating swarmer cells (with a single chromosome) does not permit gap-filling by recombination, due to absence of a homologous template for repair (Figure 1A, bottom panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and flow cytometry data showing single chromosome.

claim: Cells lacking the recombination protein RecN showed similar dynamics of β-clamp foci to that seen in wild type cells.
source: In addition, we also conducted our damage recovery experiments in cells lacking the recombination protein RecN (Vickridge et al., 2017), an essential component of recombination-based repair in Caulobacter (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015). We observed similar dynamics of β-clamp foci to that seen in wild type cells in this case as well (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reports in E. coli as well as eukaryotic systems have suggested that ssDNA gaps generated by NER can sometimes be filled by specialized polymerases like Polκ.
source: Reports in E. coli as well as eukaryotic systems (including yeast and human cells) have suggested that ssDNA gaps generated by NER can sometimes be filled by specialized polymerases like Polκ (Janel-Bintz et al., 2017; Kozmin and Jinks-Robertson, 2013; Sertic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DnaE2 is expressed in non-replicating Caulobacter cells under damage conditions.
source: Although we were unable to generate a functional fluorescent fusion to Caulobacter low-fidelity polymerase DnaE2, we confirmed that DnaE2 is expressed in our experimental conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and that deletion of dnaE2 resulted in severe sensitivity of a steady-state population of cells to MMC-treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Deletion of dnaE2 resulted in severe sensitivity of a steady-state population of cells to MMC-treatment.
source: Although we were unable to generate a functional fluorescent fusion to Caulobacter low-fidelity polymerase DnaE2, we confirmed that DnaE2 is expressed in our experimental conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and that deletion of dnaE2 resulted in severe sensitivity of a steady-state population of cells to MMC-treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In wild type cells, 52% had DnaN foci after 30 min of 0.5 µg/ml MMC treatment and this number reduced to 30% 90 min post-MMC removal.
source: For example, in case of wild type, 52% cells had foci after 30 min of 0.5 µg/ml MMC treatment and this number reduced to 30% 90 min post-MMC removal.
evidence: This is quantification from microscopy data.

claim: Replisome persistence in the absence of dnaE2 appeared to be a dose-dependent phenomenon.
source: Replisome persistence in the absence of dnaE2 appeared to be a dose-dependent phenomenon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At low dose of MMC treatment (0.125 µg/ml), fewer cells had DnaN foci post-DNA damage exposure (14.5% cells), which further reduced to 9.5% during recovery in a DnaE2-independent manner.
source: At low dose of MMC treatment (0.125 µg/ml), fewer cells had DnaN foci post-DNA damage exposure (14.5% cells). The number further reduced to 9.5% during recovery in a DnaE2-independent manner.
evidence: This is quantification from microscopy data.

claim: The percentage of cells with persistent β-clamp foci increased with increasing concentrations of damage in the absence of dnaE2, with minimal recovery observed at 0.5–0.75 µg/ml of MMC treatment.
source: However, the percentage of cells with persistent β-clamp foci increased with increasing concentrations of damage in the absence of dnaE2, with minimal recovery observed at 0.5–0.75 µg/ml of MMC treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The replicative polymerase, DnaE, was unable to dissociate during damage recovery in cells lacking dnaE2.
source: Apart from β-clamp foci, we found that the replicative polymerase, DnaE, was also unable to dissociate during damage recovery in cells lacking dnaE2 (Figure 4C), suggesting that the replicative polymerase alone cannot complete synthesis across these NER-generated ssDNA tracts.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The replicative polymerase alone cannot complete synthesis across NER-generated ssDNA tracts in non-replicating cells.
source: Apart from β-clamp foci, we found that the replicative polymerase, DnaE, was also unable to dissociate during damage recovery in cells lacking dnaE2 (Figure 4C), suggesting that the replicative polymerase alone cannot complete synthesis across these NER-generated ssDNA tracts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of persistent DnaE foci in ΔdnaE2 cells.

claim: Long ssDNA gaps persisted in the absence of DnaE2, as indicated by lack of SSB dissociation.
source: Such lack of dissociation after localization was found to be the case for SSB as well, again suggesting that long ssDNA gaps persisted in the absence of DnaE2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on microscopy data showing persistent SSB foci in ΔdnaE2 cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cells expressing catalytically inactive DnaE2 had persistent DnaN foci during damage recovery, as seen in the case of cells lacking the specialized polymerase.
source: In our experimental regime, we found that cells expressing catalytically inactive DnaE2 also had persistent DnaN foci during damage recovery, as seen in the case of cells lacking the specialized polymerase (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DnaE2 was responsible for all damage-induced mutagenesis in the experimental regimen.
source: We observed that this polymerase was responsible for all damage-induced mutagenesis in our experimental regimen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by rifampicin resistance assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Cells lacking imuB exhibited persistent DnaN foci, as seen for cells lacking dnaE2.
source: When we conducted our recovery experiments in cells lacking imuB, we observed that these cells also exhibited persistent DnaN foci, as seen for cells lacking dnaE2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DnaE2-mediated synthesis contributes to gap-filling and subsequent dissociation of replisome components in non-replicating cells.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that DnaE2-mediated synthesis contributes to gap-filling and subsequent dissociation of replisome components in non-replicating cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observations of persistent foci in ΔdnaE2, dnaE2*, and ΔimuB cells.

claim: Control cells without damage treatment and with or without an additional 90 min arrest in swarmer stage were able to robustly resume cell growth and division, with >94% cells undergoing their first division within 240 min of release into replication-permissive conditions.
source: Control cells without damage treatment and with or without an additional 90 min arrest in swarmer stage were able to robustly resume cell growth and division, with >94% cells undergoing their first division within 240 min of release into replication-permissive conditions.
evidence: This is quantification from time-lapse imaging data.

claim: In MMC-treated conditions, cells released into replication-permissive conditions immediately after damage treatment did not recover efficiently, with only 5% cells undergoing their first division within 240 min.
source: In MMC-treated conditions, we found that cells released into replication-permissive conditions immediately after damage treatment did not recover efficiently, with only 5% cells undergoing their first division within 240 min (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Wild type cells that were provided time for damage recovery before reinitiating replication showed restoration of cell division, with 30% cells undergoing at least one division and 9% cells undergoing ≥2 divisions within 240 min.
source: In contrast, wild type cells that were provided time for damage recovery before reinitiating replication showed restoration of cell division in the same time period, with 30% cells undergoing at least one division and 9% cells undergoing ≥2 divisions within 240 min (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Recovery dynamics were dependent on DnaE2 as only 7% cells lacking dnaE2 underwent divisions even when they were provided the same time duration as wild type for damage recovery before replication reinitiation.
source: These recovery dynamics were dependent on DnaE2 as only 7% cells lacking dnaE2 underwent divisions even when they were provided the same time duration as wild type for damage recovery before replication reinitiation (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: DnaE2-mediated gap-filling provided significant survival advantage to non-replicating cells as measured by their ability to robustly restore cell cycle progression and cell division.
source: Thus, DnaE2-mediated gap-filling provided significant survival advantage to non-replicating cells as measured by their ability to robustly restore cell cycle progression and cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the time-lapse imaging data showing division restoration.

claim: Cells that did not face damage (with or without dnaE2) had a median cell length of 4.6 µm after 90 min incubation in swarmer conditions.
source: We found that cells that did not face damage (with or without dnaE2) had a median cell length of 4.6 µm after 90 min incubation in swarmer conditions.
evidence: This is quantification from cell length measurement data.

claim: At 240 min after reinitiation of replication, the cell length distribution was restored close to a wild type-like pattern (control) with the median cell length dropping to 2.9 µm in undamaged cells.
source: At 240 min after reinitiation of replication, the cell length distribution was restored close to a wild type-like pattern (control) with the median cell length dropping to 2.9 µm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, 'no damage').
evidence: This is supported by cell length distribution data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Length restoration was observed in wild type cells able to engage in DnaE2-mediated gap-filling in the 90 min recovery window.
source: Length restoration was also observed in wild type cells able to engage in DnaE2-mediated gap-filling in the 90 min recovery window (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, '+ damage, recovery, wild type').
evidence: This is supported by cell length distribution data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cell length restoration was dependent on the time provided for damage recovery as well as presence of DnaE2.
source: This restoration in cell length was dependent on the time provided for damage recovery as well as presence of DnaE2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cell length distribution data.

claim: Wild type cells that were released into replication-permissive conditions without the 90 min window of damage recovery were significantly compromised in growth, with fraction survival reducing to 0.19 at higher doses of damage in the absence of recovery.
source: We observed that wild type cells that were released into replication-permissive conditions without the 90 min window of damage recovery were significantly compromised in growth, with fraction survival reducing to 0.19 at higher doses of damage in the absence of recovery.
evidence: This is supported by viable cell count data.

claim: In case of cells grown with the possibility of undergoing 90 min of damage recovery, the fraction survival increased to 0.45 at the highest dose of damage used.
source: On the other hand, in case of cells grown with the possibility of undergoing 90 min of damage recovery, the fraction survival increased to 0.45 at the highest dose of damage used (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by viable cell count data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: DnaE2 had a significant impact on the replication-independent survival advantage at higher doses of DNA damage.
source: Consistent with a dose-dependent effect on replisome persistence in the absence of DnaE2, we also observed that DnaE2 had a significant impact on the replication-independent survival advantage at higher doses of DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by viable cell count data.

claim: Cells deleted for dnaE2 were severely compromised for survival at all doses of damage used.
source: We found that cells deleted for dnaE2 were severely compromised for survival at all doses of damage used (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by viable cell count data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At higher doses of damage, cells lacking dnaE2 had similar reduction in viable cell counts whether or not they were given a 90 min window of recovery.
source: However, at higher doses of damage, cells lacking dnaE2 had similar reduction in viable cell counts whether or not they were given a 90 min window of recovery.
evidence: This is supported by viable cell count data.

claim: After treatment with 0.5 µg/ml of MMC, only 0.01 fraction survival was observed for cells lacking dnaE2 (with or without damage recovery).
source: For example, after treatment with 0.5 µg/ml of MMC, only 0.01 fraction survival was observed for cells lacking dnaE2 (with or without damage recovery).
evidence: This is quantification from viable cell count data.

claim: Wild type cells which had 90 min of damage recovery showed a fraction survival of 0.45 after treatment with 0.5 µg/ml of MMC.
source: On the other hand, wild type cells which had 90 min of damage recovery showed a fraction survival of 0.45 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is quantification from viable cell count data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was a significant component of enhanced survival in cells that could undergo repair in non-replicating conditions and this survival advantage was dependent on DnaE2.
source: Thus, there was a significant component of enhanced survival in cells that could undergo repair in non-replicating conditions and this survival advantage was dependent on DnaE2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the viable cell count data.

claim: DnaE2-mediated gap-filling enables cell cycle restoration and cell division licensing when non-replicating cells are allowed to reinitiate DNA replication.
source: In summary, our cell biological and genetic read-outs suggest that DnaE2-mediated gap-filling enables cell cycle restoration and cell division licensing when non-replicating cells are allowed to reinitiate DNA replication.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of data including time-lapse imaging, cell length measurements, and survival assays.

claim: In the absence of DnaE2-mediated recovery, cell division is compromised and cells continue to elongate, a hallmark of persistent DNA damage and continuously active SOS response.
source: In the absence of such recovery (either dnaE2 deletion or cells grown without time for recovery), cell division is compromised and cells continue to elongate, a hallmark of persistent DNA damage and hence continuously active SOS response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cell length and division data.

claim: The impact of delayed cell division and subsequent cell length elongation is directly observed when viable cell count of the population is measured, with a dose-dependent effect on survival in cells compromised for recovery due to deletion of dnaE2.
source: The impact of delayed cell division and subsequent cell length elongation is directly observed when viable cell count of the population is measured, with a dose-dependent effect on survival in cells compromised for recovery due to deletion of dnaE2.
evidence: This is a conclusion linking the cell biological observations to survival outcomes.

claim: DNA damage is a universal event that can occur across all stages of the cell cycle, including in non-replicating conditions.
source: However, DNA damage is a universal event that can occur across all stages of the cell cycle, including in non-replicating conditions.
evidence: This is general knowledge about DNA damage.

claim: DNA damage can have effects on transcription and could also perturb replication progression upon reinitiation.
source: This can have effects on transcription and could also perturb replication progression upon reinitiation (Jeiranian et al., 2013; Lang and Merrikh, 2018; Rudolph et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bacteria such as Caulobacter have distinct cell cycle phases including a non-replicating swarmer state, with a single copy of its chromosome.
source: For example, bacteria such as Caulobacter have distinct cell cycle phases including a non-replicating swarmer state, with a single copy of its chromosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Caulobacter cell cycle.

claim: It is imperative that DNA damage is repaired efficiently even in non-replicating conditions.
source: Hence, it is imperative that DNA damage is repaired efficiently even in these conditions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the potential consequences of unrepaired damage.

claim: The study provides in vivo evidence for NER-coupled DnaE2 function that is active in non-replicating bacteria.
source: Here, we provide in vivo evidence for NER-coupled DnaE2 function that is active in non-replicating bacteria.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: The study complements a growing body of work that supports the possibility of low-fidelity polymerase-mediated synthesis in replication-independent conditions across domains of life.
source: This study complements a growing body of work that supports the possibility of low-fidelity polymerase-mediated synthesis (including mutagenesis) in replication-independent conditions (such as in stationary phase cells) across domains of life (Bull et al., 2001; Corzett et al., 2013; Janel-Bintz et al., 2017; Sung et al., 2003; Yeiser et al., 2002) and underscores the need to reconsider function of such polymerases outside canonical, isolated roles of lesion bypass during replication.
evidence: This is a contextualization of the study's findings within the broader literature supported by citations.

claim: NER is thought to generate gaps of approximately 12 nucleotides during lesion repair, which can be gap-filled by DNA PolI.
source: Conventionally NER is thought to generate gaps of approximately 12 nucleotides during lesion repair, which can be gap-filled by DNA PolI (Kisker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NER mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Localization of SSB in the experiments suggests the presence of gaps > 30 nucleotides, enabling SSB tetramerization and binding.
source: However, localization of SSB in our experiments suggests the presence of gaps > 30 nucleotides, enabling SSB tetramerization and binding (Bell et al., 2015; Lohman and Ferrari, 1994).
evidence: This is an inference based on SSB localization data and established knowledge about SSB binding properties.

claim: Previous reports in E. coli as well as yeast and human cells have implicated a role for exonuclease activity in generating longer ssDNA tracts on some NER substrates.
source: Previous reports in E. coli as well as yeast and human cells have implicated a role for exonuclease activity in generating longer ssDNA tracts on some NER substrates.
evidence: This is a summary of previous literature.

claim: Exonuclease activity would occur on problematic intermediates generated during NER activity, including closely-spaced opposing lesions that are generated under high doses of DNA damage.
source: In these studies, it was proposed that such activity would occur on problematic intermediates generated during NER activity, including closely-spaced opposing lesions that are generated under high doses of DNA damage (Janel-Bintz et al., 2017; Kozmin and Jinks-Robertson, 2013; Sertic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of proposed models from previous literature supported by citations.

claim: Observations on lack of dissociation of replicative polymerase (PolIII) in the absence of DnaE2 as well as the dose-dependent impact on cell survival would be consistent with a model where NER-mediated excision results in the production of lesion-containing ssDNA that requires synthesis by a specialized polymerase.
source: Indeed, our observations on lack of dissociation of replicative polymerase (PolIII) in the absence of DnaE2 as well as the dose-dependent impact on cell survival would both be consistent with a speculative model where NER-mediated excision results in the production of lesion-containing ssDNA that requires synthesis by a specialized polymerase.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the data.

claim: It is plausible that DnaE2 contributes to gap-filling independent of the presence or absence of a DNA lesion.
source: It is equally plausible that DnaE2 contributes to gap-filling independent of the presence or absence of a DNA lesion.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

claim: Earlier studies in E. coli indicated that a minor component of NER-mediated removal of UV lesions can result in long ssDNA gaps that are gap-filled in a process referred to as long patch excision repair (LPER).
source: Earlier studies in E. coli indicated that a minor component of NER-mediated removal of UV lesions can result in long ssDNA gaps that are gap-filled in a process referred to a long patch excision repair (LPER) (Cooper, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Long patch excision repair (LPER) in E. coli did not result in detectable mutations.
source: Though the molecular players of this long patch synthesis are unidentified, this process did not result in detectable mutations.
evidence: This is information from previous literature on LPER.

claim: Studies in yeast have implicated a role for exonuclease activity (via Exo1) in generating long gaps during a subset of NER events which drive checkpoint activation and are eventually filled via long patch repair synthesis.
source: Furthermore, studies in yeast have implicated a role for exonuclease activity (via Exo1) in generating long gaps during a subset of NER events which drive checkpoint activation and are eventually filled via long patch repair synthesis (Giannattasio et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on yeast NER.

claim: DnaE2 could function in gap-filling on long ssDNA gaps formed as a consequence of extensive NER in the context of severe DNA damage.
source: DnaE2 could function similarly in gap-filling on these long ssDNA gaps formed as a consequence extensive NER in the context of severe DNA damage.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on analogy to yeast systems.

claim: Gap-filling activity has been suggested previously for specialized polymerases such as eukaryotic Polκ.
source: Gap-filling activity has been suggested previously for specialized polymerases such as eukaryotic Polκ (Ogi and Lehmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Recent studies on post-replicative gap-filling have proposed a scenario where long patches requiring synthesis are accessed by both replicative and TLS polymerases (PolIV and PolV) in E. coli.
source: In addition, recent studies on post-replicative gap-filling have proposed a scenario where long patches requiring synthesis are accessed by both replicative and TLS polymerases (PolIV and PolV) in E. coli (Isogawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: In non-replicating Caulobacter cells, it is possible that DnaE2 can access the β-clamp and hence participate in gap-filling, given the observed increase in DnaE2 levels via SOS induction.
source: In the case of non-replicating Caulobacter cells, it is possible that DnaE2 can access the β-clamp and hence participate in such gap-filling, given the observed increase in DnaE2 levels via SOS induction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing DnaE2 expression and β-clamp localization.

claim: A limitation of the current study is that not all NER events are observed, a significant proportion of which could be mediated via gap-filling by PolI on short ssDNA stretches.
source: A limitation of our current study is that we do not observe all NER events, a significant proportion of which could be mediated via gap-filling by PolI on short ssDNA stretches.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: The relative contribution of long vs. short patch repair could vary with increasing doses of damage and subsequently impact the requirement for DnaE2 action in gap-filling.
source: The relative contribution of these two arms of NER (long vs. short patch repair) could vary with increasing doses of damage and subsequently impact the requirement for DnaE2 action in gap-filling.
evidence: This is a speculation about how damage dose affects repair pathway choice.

claim: A role for DnaE2 in gap-filling alone has not been reported before.
source: It must be noted though, that a role for DnaE2 in gap-filling alone has not been reported before.
evidence: This is an assessment of the novelty of one possible interpretation of the findings.

claim: Unlike E. coli, DnaE2 is the only polymerase implicated in TLS-associated functions (mutagenesis) in the bacteria that encode it.
source: In addition, unlike E. coli, it is the only polymerase implicated in TLS-associated functions (mutagenesis) in the bacteria that encode it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DnaE2 function.

claim: The work underscores a novel and necessary function for DnaE2 in conjunction with NER in replication-independent conditions, irrespective of the specific nature of DnaE2 activity.
source: However, irrespective of the specific nature of DnaE2 activity, our work underscores a novel and necessary function for this highly conserved specialized polymerase in conjunction with NER in replication-independent conditions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Previous studies in E. coli have found that NER activity in GGR is dependent on the activation of the SOS response.
source: Previous studies in E. coli have found that NER activity in GGR is dependent on the activation of the SOS response (Crowley and Hanawalt, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The results suggest that NER functions upstream of the SOS response in non-replicating Caulobacter in the context of long patch repair.
source: In contrast, our results suggest that NER functions upstream of the SOS response in non-replicating Caulobacter in the context of long patch repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that ΔuvrA cells lack SOS induction.

claim: Although uvr genes are SOS-induced even in Caulobacter, it is possible that basal levels of Uvr proteins are sufficient to carry out damage scanning and subsequent lesion processing.
source: Although uvr genes are SOS-induced even in Caulobacter (da Rocha et al., 2008), it is possible that basal levels of Uvr proteins are sufficient to carry out damage scanning and subsequent lesion processing.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that NER occurs before SOS induction.

claim: In E. coli, basal UvrA levels are variable, but range from 9 to 43 copies in minimal media and more than 120 copies in rich media.
source: Indeed, in E. coli, basal UvrA levels are variable, but range from 9 to 43 copies in minimal media and more than 120 copies in rich media (Ghodke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on UvrA levels.

claim: In case of Caulobacter, RecA is likely essential only for turning on the SOS regulon as DnaE2-mediated synthesis has been previously shown to function independent of RecA.
source: it is likely that in case of Caulobacter, RecA is essential only for turning on the SOS regulon as DnaE2-mediated synthesis has been previously shown to function independent of RecA (Alves et al., 2017; Galhardo et al., 2005), unlike E. coli PolV (Goodman, 2014; Nohmi et al., 1988).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and previous literature supported by citations.

claim: SSB localization on ssDNA could facilitate recruitment and loading of the PolIIIHE.
source: SSB localization on ssDNA could further facilitate recruitment and loading of the PolIIIHE.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of replisome loading.

claim: PolIII activity could directly contribute to gap-filling.
